cards.title: Diagnose Which Off-Site Channels Own Your Category Queries
cards.summary: Map the recurring top-10 domains (marketplaces, publishers, review sites, forums) across a category's head queries to find the channels worth attacking.
cards.use_when: Planning which channels to invest in (Amazon, third-party review content, earned placements) for a product category you want to rank in.
steps: Pull the top 10 results for your core buy-intent queries (e.g. 'best creatine for vegans') and note the recurring entities: Healthline, Amazon, Reddit, Forbes, Garage Gym Reviews type domains.

Flag which of those you already have a presence on. In the source example, the brand sold some products on Amazon but had withheld its flagship creatine — the presenter flags that as a self-inflicted visibility gap worth reversing.
Check whether the marketplace itself appears as a ranking entity for the topic; if Amazon ranks, listing there is a second channel to attack, not just a distribution decision.
Count how many of the top 10 you have any coverage on. The source treats 20% brand coverage across those entities as a rough tipping point for movement, because the current bar is low.
Prioritise earned placements and marketplace presence for the entities you cannot outrank with owned pages.
Re-run the entity audit each quarter since the mix of domains ranking for a category shifts.
caveats: The 20% coverage figure is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Listing on a marketplace can conflict with brand positioning; treat it as a strategic trade-off, not an automatic win.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Choose Blog vs Category Page for a Long-Tail Commercial Query
cards.summary: Before building content for a niche query, search your own site to decide whether a new category page would duplicate an existing one.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to publish content targeting a modifier query such as 'best creatine for vegans' or 'creatine for sensitive stomachs'.
steps: Search your own domain for the modifier plus your product (e.g. brand + 'vegan', 'vegan creatine', 'vegan-friendly supplements').
If a slightly broader category page already covers the topic, do not build a near-duplicate category page for the narrow variant.
Publish the asset as blog/listicle content instead, linking into the existing category page rather than competing with it.
If no existing page is close, a category page is viable — but confirm the query volume justifies a permanent collection page rather than an article.
Keep each modifier query as its own asset; the source stresses these are not duplicates because each surfaces a different competitor set.
Route link equity from each article back to the central category page so the category accumulates authority.
caveats: The source's example is a supplement brand; the blog-vs-category decision depends on whether a suitable parent collection already exists.
Do not assume keyword cannibalisation is harmless — confirm the parent page is not already ranking for the variant.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Brief an AI Listicle with Your Brand Placed First
cards.summary: Ground an AI-generated comparison listicle by specifying your product as the number-one recommendation and feeding it real differentiators.
cards.use_when: Producing 'best X for Y' listicle content where you want your product to be the top pick.
steps: Enter the target query, language/region, and a custom instruction such as 'rank [Brand]'s [product] as the number one for [use case]'.
Confirm the system has detected discover/commercial-investigation intent, and select which search platforms to research (Google plus AI citation sources if you want broader coverage).

Generate the differentiators rather than writing them by hand: ask an AI assistant for three to four sentences on how the brand uniquely differs, then for 5–10 unique differentiators versus competitors as a simple list.
Paste those differentiators into the brief with the clarification that they apply to the brand that should be ranked number one.
Set up a brand voice profile in settings before running campaigns so the draft inherits it.
Add brand terms and associated entities (e.g. founders' names) so the model links the brand to the right knowledge.
Accept the returned brief, check that your product appears first in the structure, then generate the draft from the brief.
caveats: Feeding your own brand as the 'number one' is a positioning instruction, not a factual claim the AI verifies.
Differentiators must be real and defensible; a fabricated advantage will read as marketing filler.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Mine AI-Built Briefs for Entities, Questions and Gaps
cards.summary: Use the generated brief to capture competitor-derived entities, People Also Ask questions and coverage gaps before writing.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a content brief before drafting a comparison or category-support article.
steps: Read the suggested title tag, meta description and URL, and keep them if they match your URL conventions.
Extract the entity list the brief pulled from competitors (often derived from 50–75 pages/articles) and treat it as your coverage checklist.
Look for the gap analysis the tool produced — topics competitors cover that you don't.
Capture the People Also Ask questions and put them into an FAQ section to capture fan-out / long-tail queries from the same asset.
After publishing, measure the individual FAQ queries; if one underperforms, split it off into a dedicated asset.
Check the internal links the brief suggests, and add one to your core category page in addition to product links.
caveats: Entity counts (e.g. ~66 covered) are output from the specific tool in the demo, not a target to hit.
FAQ fan-out performance should be measured per query rather than judged as a whole.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Treat AI Drafts as First Drafts: Fact-Check and Restructure
cards.summary: AI listicles need explicit numbers, verified facts and tighter formatting before production.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a generated product comparison draft before publishing to a PDP-adjacent or blog asset.
steps: Scan for hedged placeholders such as 'contact for pricing' and replace them with specific, accurate figures — the source flags vague pricing as unacceptable in a listicle.
Recognise that the model often plays it safe; where a fact is available it may retrieve it, but where uncertain it will hedge, so verify each numeric or technical claim.
Note that the workflow layers additional web research on top of competitor extraction specifically to confirm facts — check which claims were verified and which were not.
Restructure bulky sections: the source recommends splitting dense passages for readability.
Expect roughly three to five revision passes before the draft is production-ready.
Use leftover unused entities/topics as seeds for further supporting content rather than stuffing them into the same asset.
caveats: The three-to-five-iteration count is the presenter's own workflow norm, not a measured average.
Verified-looking retrieved facts still need a human check before publication.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Run a Page-Level Audit for Both Search and AI Retrieval
cards.summary: Audit an existing category or product page across crawl, content, structure, freshness, performance and agent-readiness before optimising.
cards.use_when: Improving an underperforming category page or product page so it ranks in traditional search and is usable as an AI retrieval source.
steps: Extract the target URL and review topic coverage — the source's example category page missed several critical topics for its core keyword.
Check crawling and indexing fundamentals, on-page structure, and content freshness.
Inspect file freshness by viewing page source and hunting stale dates (e.g. 2022/2023 timestamps); AI platforms parse your code, not your design, so outdated markup and assets matter.
Review UX and performance signals such as load speed — slow pages are penalised in both traditional and AI retrieval.
Run the page through a helpful-content-based quality assessment and act on the recommendations.
Treat the audit list as layered: satisfying crawl, content and structure helps traditional ranking, AI retrieval and model inclusion.
Prioritise the biggest gap first rather than working top to bottom.
caveats: The claim that the tool covers ~99.9% of needed variables is vendor positioning.
Freshness preference in AI retrieval is stated by the presenter as an observed pattern, not a documented ranking factor.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Get Indexed by CCBot to Be Baked Into AI Training
cards.summary: Ensure Common Crawl's crawler can access your store so your pages can enter the datasets used to train language models.
cards.use_when: Setting crawl policy, robots rules or bot access for an ecommerce site that wants long-term AI visibility.
steps: Allow CCBot (Common Crawl's bot) to crawl your key commercial pages; CCBot builds a monthly open snapshot of the web that model providers download.
Understand the two-tier outcome: retrieval means an AI agent finds your page live during a query, while being 'baked into the model' means your content was part of training — the source wants both.
Verify your robots.txt and bot-level rules (including those aimed at AI crawlers) are not blocking these agents.
Add agent-friendly enhancements to pages so bots can parse and navigate the site: clean structure and machine-readable content such as a markdown version.
Implement the fix mechanically: download the audit's markdown, hand it to an AI assistant and ask it to generate the agent-readiness changes — the source reports doing this in under an hour.
Re-audit the page afterwards to confirm the agentic variables are now in place.
caveats: The presenter says he remains somewhat sceptical about markdown versions of pages.
The '60% of searches are agents' figure is the speaker's estimate, not a published statistic.
Model providers filter the Common Crawl download heavily, so crawling access does not guarantee inclusion in training data.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Optimise for Agent Navigation, Not Just Human Design
cards.summary: Make your storefront machine-navigable because a growing share of queries are resolved by bots that deconstruct your code.
cards.use_when: Prioritising a technical roadmap for a store where AI assistants and crawlers may be the first visitor to a product or category page.
steps: Assume agents read source code — layout polish is irrelevant to them; structure, semantics and data clarity are what matter.
Provide clean internal linking so a bot can move from a listicle or FAQ to the category and product pages.
Keep structured, retrievable facts on product pages: specs, prices, ingredient or material details — the source criticises hedged 'contact for pricing' content.
Ship a machine-readable representation of key pages (e.g. markdown) if you can generate it cheaply, while accepting the source's own reservations about it.
Balance investment between human UX and agent UX; the presenter argues for leaning slightly toward agents given the volume shift.
Re-check agent-accessibility after any major site change or CMS migration.
caveats: The presenter's lean-toward-agents stance is an opinion about relative allocation, not a measured optimum.
Markdown and similar techniques are described as speculative upside.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Build a Hub-and-Spoke Content System Around the Category Page
cards.summary: Publish modifier-query assets that all link back to a central category page to concentrate authority.
cards.use_when: Structuring content coverage for a product line where multiple niche variants drive searches.
steps: Identify the core category page and treat it as the hub that must receive link equity.
Publish a separate asset per modifier query (vegan, sensitive stomach, budget, etc.) rather than one giant page.
Internally link every article to at least one other related asset and to the category page.
Brief each article independently, because each query surfaces a different competitor set and therefore a genuinely different asset.
Add the category-page internal link to the standard brief checklist so it is never skipped.
Repeat the same production process for every asset so output is consistent.
caveats: The source claims these assets are inherently non-duplicative because competitor sets differ; still check for overlapping coverage before publishing.
Too many near-identical spokes can dilute rather than concentrate authority.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Reframe Search Strategy as Full Digital Marketing
cards.summary: Search visibility now depends on on-site quality plus off-site presence, so budget both, not just SEO tactics.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget and headcount between on-site content and off-site earned/marketplace work for a store's search programme.
steps: Split the plan into owned content (category pages, product pages, articles) and earned content (placements, reviews, forum and publisher coverage).
Accept that a meaningful share of the work is off-site; the source's own walkthrough devotes substantial time to entities you do not control.
Sequence owned work first only where it is genuinely fast to fix (technical gaps, missing entities), then pursue earned placements for high-influence domains.
Set expectations that visible movement from owned content alone is limited when third-party domains dominate the top 10.
Track both channels, since AI retrieval draws on publisher and forum sources as well as your site.
caveats: The source offers no cost or ROI benchmarks for earned placements.
This is the presenter's strategic framing, not a tested channel-mix model.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Benchmark and Competitor Reports to Scope a Category
cards.summary: Establish current visibility benchmarks and identify top competitors before deciding what content to build.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a search programme for a new product category and needing a baseline.
steps: Run a benchmark report for the target category to record current visibility before any changes.
Identify the top competitors ranking for the category's core queries.
Compare at category level rather than query by query, so the plan targets the whole topic cluster.
Cross-check the competitor list against the entity audit of top-10 results to see which competitors appear as domains versus as cited entities.
Use the gap between your benchmark and the competitor set to prioritise which assets to build first.
Re-benchmark after shipping the first wave to judge whether the approach is moving visibility.
caveats: The source does not specify which visibility metric the benchmark uses.
Baseline comparisons are only meaningful if the query set stays constant between runs.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce SEO_ The Definitive Guide for 2026.docx
